title: The world’s top 10 cities by economic strength in 2026
gist: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index scores 1,000 cities on a six-measure Economics composite (GDP size, GDP growth, stability, GDP per capita, employment growth, diversity), and finds nine of the top 10 economic cities are American, with New York first on a metro economy nearly double Tokyo's or LA's. Beneath the incumbents, AI- and trade-driven mid-sized cities — Hsinchu, Kuala Lumpur, Shenzhen, Bengaluru, Ho Chi Minh City, Riyadh, Port Said and Suez — are closing the gap fastest.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' Global Cities Index ranks the 1,000 largest cities across five categories — Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment and Governance — with the Economics score itself built from six measures: GDP size, GDP growth, economic stability, GDP per capita, employment growth, and economic diversity.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for site selection, municipal credit and regional allocation: it separates cities that are merely big from those that are big, stable and broadly prosperous.
insights.quote: GDP size, GDP growth, economic stability, GDP per capita, employment growth, and economic diversity
insights.locator: Economics sits at the heart of

insights.claim: Single-metric city rankings mislead because a city can be fast-growing but volatile, or enormous but stagnant — only a composite identifies which cities are best placed to stay economically vital over the long term.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Warns against headline-GDP or headline-growth screens when underwriting long-duration urban exposure such as real estate or infrastructure.
insights.quote: A city can be fast-growing but volatile, or enormous but stagnant.
insights.locator: This composite approach matters because

insights.claim: Economic staying power comes from two opposite directions at once: the largest metros defend position through scale, stability and compounding agglomeration effects, while smaller fast-growing cities close the gap riding demographic and sectoral tailwinds.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Supports a barbell in urban exposure — core mega-metros for stability plus a selective sleeve of high-growth mid-sized cities — rather than a single-tier bet.
insights.quote: opportunity isn’t confined to any one tier or type of city, but knowing how to capitalise on it is what will decide who’s still climbing next year
insights.locator: Scale, speed, and staying power

insights.claim: Large incumbent cities repeat at the top of rankings year after year because their sheer scale means even small percentage gains translate into large absolute increases, even though their GDP growth rates are more modest than smaller emerging cities'.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Explains why absolute-dollar opportunity and percentage-growth opportunity point to entirely different city lists — pick the metric that matches the strategy.
insights.locator: While these cities differ in their specific strengths

insights.claim: The virtuous cycle behind dominant city economies runs: productive sectors generate high incomes per person, which attract productive workers, who in turn contribute to the economy.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Identifies talent inflow as the leading indicator to watch for whether a top-tier city is holding or losing its economic moat.
insights.quote: productive sectors that generate high incomes per person, which in turn attract productive workers, who contribute to the economy, creating a virtuous cycle
insights.locator: While these cities differ in their specific strengths

themes.theme: US dominance of the Economics table

insights.claim: Nine of the ten top-ranked cities by Economics score are in the United States — New York, Los Angeles, San Jose, Seattle, San Francisco, Dallas, Washington DC, Boston and Houston — with London the only non-US entrant, at seventh.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: An argument for US-centric urban and metro-level exposure; non-US city allocations rest on categories other than raw economic strength.
insights.quote: Nine of our top 10 cities by Economics rankings are in the US, with London the sole non-US city to break into the group.
insights.locator: And New York is far from alone at the top

insights.claim: New York holds the world's biggest metro economy at nearly double the size of the next-largest cities, Tokyo and Los Angeles, and combines it with remarkably stable long-term GDP dynamics.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Quantifies the gap incumbents would have to close and underpins New York's status as the default core urban allocation.
insights.quote: nearly double that of the next-largest cities, Tokyo and Los Angeles
insights.locator: New York takes top spot

insights.claim: New York's economic diversity score is lower than peers' because of the outsized role of its finance sector, yet Oxford Economics still expects it to remain a top-scoring city for years to come.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Flags concentration risk: a severe financial-sector shock is the single identified channel that could dent New York's ranking.
insights.locator: New York takes top spot

insights.claim: San Jose ranks third on Economics and records the highest GDP per person of all 1,000 cities in the index, driven by a dense concentration of tech heavyweights including Apple's headquarters.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Confirms tech-cluster rents accrue to a very narrow geography — relevant for Bay Area property, wage and local tax-base exposure.
insights.locator: And New York is far from alone at the top

insights.claim: Los Angeles takes second place on a broad economic base spanning entertainment, tech and aerospace that has driven high GDP per person — economic breadth, not a single sector, is its ranking driver.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Sector-diversified metros can rank near the top without a single dominant industry, a useful contrast to San Jose's concentration.
insights.locator: And New York is far from alone at the top

themes.theme: US vs Europe: different sources of advantage

insights.claim: The US accounts for 30 of the top 100 cities in the index, and its dominance comes from Economics and Human Capital scores, whereas European cities' elevated positions come from Quality of Life, Environmental and Governance categories.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Europe's city ranking strength is amenity-led rather than growth-led — a caution for anyone reading headline European city rankings as a growth signal.
insights.quote: In the US, it is strong scores across the Economics and Human Capital categories that drive their elevated position. In Europe, however, it is outperformance across the Quality of Life, Environmental, and Governance categories.
insights.locator: As is immediately visible, cities across North America

insights.claim: London is the fourth-biggest city economy in the world by GDP and Europe's premier economic powerhouse, backed by a long track record of stable growth, while Paris ranks fifth-biggest by GDP on a service-oriented economy but places only 13th on Economics.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Size and score diverge in Europe — Paris's GDP scale does not buy a top-10 Economics ranking, so scale alone is not the European investment case.
insights.locator: Over in Europe, London remains

insights.claim: Dublin's third-highest GDP per capita in the world is inflated by large multinationals booking operations there and should be interpreted with caution, though its underlying indicators — robust employment growth across tech, finance and pharmaceuticals — remain strong.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Discount headline Irish per-capita GDP in any city comparison and use employment growth instead; multinational accounting distortion is the known artefact.
insights.quote: this figure is being inflated by the presence of large multinationals whose operations are located there
insights.locator: Dublin’s position needs to be interpreted

themes.theme: AI as the Asian growth engine

insights.claim: Hsinchu, 70 km southwest of Taipei, is showing the most significant AI-related growth of any Asian city and is one of Asia's fastest-growing cities by GDP, powered by rising demand for AI-linked chip exports.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Names the single geography most levered to AI chip demand — a real-economy read-through for Taiwan semiconductor supply-chain exposure and a concentration risk if AI capex slows.
insights.quote: powered by rising demand for AI-linked chip exports
insights.locator: The global AI boom is playing a huge part

insights.claim: Kuala Lumpur is closing in on a top-50 index spot as Malaysia's leading digital hub, hosting roughly half the country's data centres and drawing multibillion-dollar investments from Google and Amazon Web Services.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of hyperscaler capex landing in Southeast Asia — watch Malaysian power, land and construction beneficiaries of data-centre buildout.
insights.locator: The global AI boom is playing a huge part

insights.claim: Shenzhen remains mainland China's top-ranked city in the index, home to Huawei and Tencent plus a dense cluster of robotics and AI businesses.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Identifies where China's AI and robotics economic activity is concentrated for anyone mapping mainland tech exposure.
insights.locator: The global AI boom is playing a huge part

insights.claim: Bengaluru has been expanding at breakneck speed on the back of its IT sector and is now poised to move into more advanced fields because of AI.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: An implied upgrade path for Indian IT from services delivery toward higher-value AI work — a thesis to test against Indian IT services earnings mix.
insights.locator: Looking just a bit further down the rankings

insights.claim: The AI boom driving city growth is described as relatively concentrated rather than broadly distributed, with a handful of named hubs capturing it.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Argues against diffuse AI-driven regional plays; the economic gains cluster in a short list of cities, so exposure should be targeted.
insights.quote: Although the AI boom is relatively concentrated, economic growth is not only centred in Asia.
insights.locator: Although the AI boom is relatively concentrated

insights.claim: Ho Chi Minh City has leveraged rising trade activity, higher-value manufacturing and an expanding private sector into GDP growth that places it in the top 5% of the index on that metric.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Quantifies Vietnam's manufacturing-shift dividend at city level — supportive of Vietnam trade, industrial property and logistics exposure.
insights.locator: Looking just a bit further down the rankings

insights.claim: Egypt's Port Said and Suez record the second- and third-fastest GDP growth rates in the entire 1,000-city index, both benefiting from their location along the Suez Canal corridor, while Cairo remains Egypt's main economic pillar on the strength of its information and communications sector.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Ties two of the world's fastest-growing city economies directly to Suez Canal throughput — Red Sea shipping disruption is therefore a direct macro risk to Egypt's fastest-growing metros.
insights.locator: Although the AI boom is relatively concentrated

insights.claim: Dakar and Nairobi face a wave of young workers entering the labour market at the same time as their economies diversify, and are positioned to expand for years if they can harness this demographic dividend.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A conditional, not assured, growth case for African frontier cities — the demographic dividend must be absorbed by jobs to convert into economic growth.
insights.locator: Elsewhere, cities such as Dakar in Senegal

insights.claim: Lima is the top-ranking South American city on Economics but only at 183rd place, and on rapid 20-year population growth plus a deepening skills base is forecast to significantly outpace regional peers on both GDP and income growth over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Shows how far South America sits from the global economic frontier — even its best city ranks 183rd — while flagging Lima as the region's relative-growth pick.
insights.locator: Latin America also has several strong performers

insights.claim: Riyadh already ranks 18th in the Economics category on large GDP size and fast employment growth, and Oxford Economics expects it to become both a megacity and an urban economic powerhouse by 2050 as Saudi Arabia moves away from oil.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A multi-decade construction, services and consumption growth story; Riyadh at 18th already outranks every South American and most Asian cities on Economics.
insights.locator: Yet no list of emerging entrants

insights.claim: Abu Dhabi is recording rapid growth as it diversifies beyond oil into finance, culture and advanced manufacturing, while Dubai's expanding financial services sector is propelling it toward becoming the world's 60th-largest city economy by 2050 — and rather than competing, the two emirates increasingly complement one another.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Reframes the standard Abu Dhabi-versus-Dubai rivalry narrative as complementarity, and puts a dated marker (60th-largest by 2050) on Dubai's financial-sector build-out.
insights.quote: Rather than competing, the two emirates increasingly complement one another’s strengths.
insights.locator: Yet no list of emerging entrants
